# 新一代无线技术加速企业创新与转型

过去三十多年里，无线互联网连接经历了翻天覆地的变化，人们对高速连接的期望，以及人与物、物与物的通信速率和效率推动着新无线技术的变革。如今，随着5G和Wi-Fi 6等新一代无线技术的完善和广泛应用，数十亿智能设备层层依联网，工业设备以及人工智能软件和机器人工具网络。物联网设备呈现指数增长，意味着这个时代对网络系统的需求达到了前所未有的高度，无线宽带技术投资布局已经成为全球企业的关键发展目标。

2020年新冠疫情席卷全球，全球企业经营受到冲击，为了解如何迎接全球化时代的先进无线技术新机遇，德勤对全球的网络技术高管展开调研。在这项调研中我们着重研究了三个板块，调查结果显示高管们对于先进无线技术的持续投资。先进无线技术对企业创新和转型的推动作用，以及技术落地带来的商业价值至关重要。在调研过程中，全球网络技术高管普遍表示出对于先进无线技术的重视。他们认为5G和Wi-Fi 6将成为商业成功的关键助力，新冠疫情期间，网络设施建设也以支持遥办公、在线学习和日常沟通等需求增长。先进无线技术正当其时，对安全、优质、无处不在的网络连接的诉求。

此外，5G和Wi-Fi 6的扩展用途也为我们揭示，作为新取数策略和采用先进无线技术的前沿之一，中国的5G采用率高达70%，Wi-Fi 6部署及试点比例（72%）也处于最高水平。2020年5月，国务院出台加快5G网络、数据中心等新型基础设施建设进度。在各方支持下，2020年底5G市场总投资超过718.7万亿元，5G基站数目超过81万个，覆盖超过300个以上城市5G网络全覆盖。2020年同期，中国WLAN市场总体规模达到7.4亿美元，而5G占总共WLAN市场31.2%，预计增长至7.2亿美元。记者对未来的技术需求非常乐观，甚至未来很长的一段时间内，5G和Wi-Fi 6将相互补充，实现无缝协作，应用在工业互联网、物联网、智能驾驶等诸多领域，帮助各行各业爆发出新的活力。

我们在谈及创新和企业转型时，许多网络技术高管对先进无线技术寄予厚望。他们认为先进无线技术对其所在企业的智慧物联网、大数据分析、人工智能、边缘计算和云计算非常重要，在企业数字化转型过程中不可或缺。中国的网络技术高管普遍希望借助先进无线技术来开发新产品和服务，这一比例达48%。除此之外，利用新技术以及提高效率也是中国企业希望实现的两个目标。

可以肯定的是，先进无线技术将以惊人的速度，以及低延时、高带宽和低延时特性，帮助企业提升智能，改变数据和业务的分析和预测，催生创新解决方案并推动企业创新周期，为社会各领域带来深刻变化。站在更宽的角度来看，作为网络发展最有的先进无线技术，将结合人工智能、数据和区块链技术，推进人类社会从“信息化”迈向“智能化”新时代。

Madera Canyon. Stephan’s riffle beetle is no longer found at the Bog Springs Campground location, as the habitat there no longer exists. Stephan’s riffle beetle has not been collected or documented since 1993, despite the Service’s surveying for the species at the one remaining known location, Sylvester Spring, and at numerous other nearby locations with potential habitat. Based on our review of the best available scientific and commercial information, we believe that the Stephan’s riffle beetle is extinct.

The preponderance of Stephan’s riffle beetle specimens have been documented in artificial habitat created by a water tank’s leaking pipeline and overflow at the Bog Springs Campground. Only two specimens have ever been documented from Sylvester Spring, the only relatively intact spring habitat now remaining where the species was known to exist. Historically, Stephan’s riffle beetle may have only occupied Sylvester and Bog Springs, and populations may have started declining when water from springs in Madera Canyon was first captured in concrete boxes and piped to divert water for domestic and recreational water supplies. Up until 1993, when Stephan’s riffle beetle was last detected, the species appears to have existed only in extremely low numbers within Sylvester Spring, making it very difficult to detect, in contrast to the relatively large numbers collected in 1979 at the Bog Springs Campground site. The species has not been documented at any site since 1993, 23 years ago, when one individual was found at Sylvester Spring as part of a specific survey to look for Stephan’s riffle beetle at Sylvester Spring and Bog Spring. Beginning in 2012, the Service surveyed Sylvester Spring, the one remaining known population location for Stephan’s riffle beetle, and several other locations with potential habitat on multiple occasions. The Service’s survey efforts have focused on Sylvester Spring and Bog Springs, the water source for the former Bog Springs Campground population. Various different survey methods were used in an effort to find the species, and no Stephan’s riffle beetles were found. Stephan’s riffle beetle is a small in size and (therefore, difficult to find), and all beetle species, should be surveyed for at least 10 years over 10 surveyed hectares of their life history (multi-year and multi-life stage) to detect a species. Based on the best available scientific and commercial information, the Service believes Stephan’s riffle beetle to be extinct.

### Summary of Status Review

The SSA Report for Stephan’s riffle beetle is a summary of the information assembled and reviewed by the Service and incorporates the best available scientific and commercial information for this species. Our analysis leads us to believe Stephan’s riffle beetle is extinct. Species extinction, as defined by the Service, is when a species is no longer in existence. Although the Service has no policy specifically defining the level of information necessary to conclude that a species should be considered extinct, for any species there is uncertainty in drawing a conclusion of extinction. For the Stephan’s riffle beetle, we have carefully assessed the best scientific and commercial information available regarding the species’ status and have reviewed the historical information regarding the biology and status of the species. This biological information was gathered and analyzed as the basis for our findings is documented in the SSA Report. Our analysis of this information found that there has been no confirmation of the existence of the Stephan’s riffle beetle in more than 23 years, despite multiple survey efforts since 2012 in known and potential habitat where other riffle beetles were documented, across multiple seasons, and using a variety of survey methods. The type locality consisting of a leaking pipeline and water storage tank, where the largest number of Stephan’s riffle beetle was collected, no longer exists. The location where the only Stephan’s riffle beetle has been documented, Sylvester Spring, and numerous occasions, despite our best survey and monitoring efforts, we have been unable to confirm the existence of the species.

### Finding

Our review of the best available scientific and commercial information indicates that the Stephan’s riffle beetle is not extinct and is no longer a candidate for listing under the Endangered Species Act. Although the loss of historical habitat decreases the situation and threats to the species, the best available scientific and commercial information indicates that the species is likely extinct. As such, the species is not an endangered species or a threatened species, by definition, under the Act. The Act defines an endangered species as a species in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range, and a threatened species as a species likely to become endangered within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range. We find that listing Stephan’s riffle beetle as an endangered or threatened species as an endangered or threatened species is not warranted. The Act is not warranted because the best available scientific and commercial information indicates that the species is extinct. As a result of the Service’s 2011 settlement agreement with the Center for Biological Diversity and WildEarth Guardians, the Service is required to conduct a 12-month finding on the Federal Register by September 30, 2016, to propose listing under the Endangered Species Act Section 4. Deadlines Litigation, No. 10–377 (EGS), MDL Docket No. 2165 (D.D.C. May 10, 2011)]. As a result of the Service’s 12-month finding on the May 4, 2004, petition to list Stephan’s riffle beetle as an endangered species, the Service has determined that listing Stephan’s riffle beetle as an endangered or threatened species is not warranted. A detailed discussion of the basis for this finding is provided in the species-specific assessment form, SSA Report, and other supporting documents (see ADDRESSES, above).

In March 2013, 24 4-m long hybrid poplar cuttings of the Grimminge cultivar \[ \textit{Populus deltoides} \times (\textit{Populus trichocarpa} \times \textit{Populus deltoides}) \] were planted on the field for future phytoremediation purposes. These trees were distributed over a defined rectangular grid of 10 m by 35 m, enclosing the area with the highest concentrations of chlorendic acid in the groundwater (> 100 mg l\(^{-1}\)) (Figure 1). In 2015, samples for isolation of cultivable fungal strains were collected from soil, rhizosphere and roots of common bent and hybrid poplar. Four soil samples were taken in a 1-m perimeter around observation wells OW175-4 and OW149-4 (Figure 1), from surface soil, \(-1\), \(-1.5\), and \(-2\) m. Common bent rhizosphere and roots were sampled inside the 1-m perimeter around each of the observation wells. Poplar rhizosphere and root samples were taken from three trees growing in the areas with high concentrations of chlorendic acid (Figure 1). From each tree, four sample repetitions were taken. In total, 32 soil samples were collected (4 × 4 depths × 2 locations), 8 bentgrass root and rhizosphere samples (4 × 2 locations) and 12 poplar rhizosphere and root samples (4 × 3 trees). Soil samples were taken with sterile tools and transported in sterile bags. Roots were collected with soil particles still adhering to the surface, which was considered the rhizosphere fraction. For poplar, the tertiary fine roots were selected. Roots within the rhizosphere fraction were obtained with sterile tools and directly transferred into falcon tubes with 30 ml sterile 10 mM MgSO\(_4\).

### Isolation of Bacteria and Fungi

Soil samples were homogenized and vortexed in sterile 10 mM MgSO\(_4\) prior to isolations. Root and rhizosphere samples were vortexed after which the roots were removed from the MgSO\(_4\). The resulting soil pellet after centrifugation (15 min, 2700g) constituted the rhizosphere fraction. Poplar roots were surface sterilized by immersing them for 5 min in 1% NaClO and bunchgrass roots were sterilized with 0.1% NaClO supplemented with 0.1% Tween. Following treatment, all roots were rinsed four times in sterile distilled water. The last rinsing solution was plated on 869 medium (Meyer et al., 1985) to confirm surface sterility by scoring microbial growth after 7 days of incubation at 30°C. The surface sterilized roots were assembled in 15 ml sterile 10 mM MgSO\(_4\) and mixed for 1 min using a Polytron PR1200 mixer (Kinematica AG).

For fungal isolations, dilutions up to 10\(^{-4}\) of the rhizosphere and endophytic root solutions were plated onto peptone-glucose-acid-agar medium pH 5, as described by Dietrich and Lamar (1990), and incubated for 7 days at 23°C.
